## PG-01 · VM stuck in BUILD? Look at the network before you look at Nova.

Image: [`dist/pg-01-vm-stuck-in-build.png`](dist/pg-01-vm-stuck-in-build.png)

```text
An instance sits in BUILD / spawning for five minutes, then goes to ERROR.

The reflex is to blame Nova. But scheduling already succeeded: a host was selected and Placement holds the allocation. nova-compute is waiting for one event from Neutron, network-vif-plugged, and it never arrives.

Three read-only checks tell you where it stopped:
→ the fault and the selected host
→ the port: binding_failed, or bound but DOWN?
→ the networking agent on that host

Deleting and recreating will not help while the agent on the host is not wiring ports.

The lesson: a networking problem wearing a compute symptom.

Runbook: https://github.com/OzarLand/openstack-vm-runbooks/blob/main/lifecycle/instance-stuck-in-build-waiting-for-vif-plugged.md
More memos: https://github.com/OzarLand/production-guide

#OpenStack #Nova #Neutron #CloudOperations #SRE #OzarLand
```

## PG-02 · "No valid host was found" is not one failure. It is three.

Image: [`dist/pg-02-no-valid-host.png`](dist/pg-02-no-valid-host.png)

```text
Capacity exists. Hypervisors have free CPU, memory and disk. And every build still ends with "No valid host was found".

Before opening a capacity ticket, read the exact message. It tells you where the request stopped:

→ "...There are not enough hosts available." A scheduler filter rejected every host. The scheduler log names it.
→ "No valid host was found." and nothing after: Placement returned no candidate. Look at inventory, allocation ratios, reserved values, disabled computes.
→ "Host '<host>' is not mapped to any cell": the compute exists but was never mapped. Classic after adding hosts.

Three causes, three different fixes, one message that looks the same at a glance.

Runbook: https://github.com/OzarLand/openstack-vm-runbooks/blob/main/scheduling/no-valid-host-with-free-capacity.md
More memos: https://github.com/OzarLand/production-guide

#OpenStack #Nova #Placement #CloudOperations #SRE #OzarLand
```

## PG-03 · "Exceeded maximum number of retries" tells you nothing. The computes do.

Image: [`dist/pg-03-max-retries-exceeded.png`](dist/pg-03-max-retries-exceeded.png)

```text
"Exceeded maximum number of retries. Exhausted all hosts available for retrying build failures."

This fault is not a scheduling failure. The scheduler found hosts. Each one tried to spawn the instance, failed, and Nova moved on to the next alternate until none was left.

So the message is a summary. The cause is the exception each compute logged, and it is usually the same on all of them:
→ one broken compute: builds succeed elsewhere, just slower
→ a shared dependency: every attempt fails the same way
→ a request no host can satisfy at spawn time

Start with `openstack server event list`, then read nova-compute.log on each host that tried.

Runbook: https://github.com/OzarLand/openstack-vm-runbooks/blob/main/scheduling/build-fails-exceeded-maximum-number-of-retries.md
More memos: https://github.com/OzarLand/production-guide

#OpenStack #Nova #Troubleshooting #CloudOperations #SRE #OzarLand
```

## PG-04 · VM stuck in deleting: why deleting it again does nothing

Image: [`dist/pg-04-vm-stuck-in-deleting.png`](dist/pg-04-vm-stuck-in-deleting.png)

```text
An instance stays in task_state "deleting". You run the delete again. Nothing changes.

That is by design: while the compute is up, Nova ignores a second delete for an instance already in deleting.

What matters is which of two paths the delete takes:
→ Compute service UP: the API hands the delete to nova-compute, which destroys the guest and frees ports, volumes and the allocation. Stuck means the compute never got the request, or never finished it.
→ Compute service DOWN: a local delete. The records go, nothing is done on the host. If that host is not really dead, the guest keeps running.

The shortcuts (virsh undefine, a database edit) leave four services with records that no longer match reality.

Runbook: https://github.com/OzarLand/openstack-vm-runbooks/blob/main/lifecycle/instance-stuck-in-deleting.md
More memos: https://github.com/OzarLand/production-guide

#OpenStack #Nova #Troubleshooting #CloudOperations #SRE #OzarLand
```

## PG-05 · ACTIVE in Nova, frozen for the user: the silent full disk

Image: [`dist/pg-05-active-but-frozen.png`](dist/pg-05-active-but-frozen.png)

```text
A user says their VM "hangs". Nova says ACTIVE. No fault, no error in the logs.

The compute's instance store is full. QEMU paused the instance on its next write, and it will wait there, losing nothing, until someone resumes it.

Three views of the same instance:
→ Nova status: ACTIVE
→ Nova power state: Paused (the only signal in Nova)
→ libvirt: paused (I/O error)

Placement does not help: it counts the disk of flavors, not the space guests actually use, so the scheduler keeps placing instances on the full host.

Freeing space is not enough. The domains stay paused until they are resumed.

Monitor the instance store, and alert on "ACTIVE but Paused".

Runbook: https://github.com/OzarLand/openstack-vm-runbooks/blob/main/lifecycle/compute-disk-full-instance-paused.md
More memos: https://github.com/OzarLand/production-guide

#OpenStack #Nova #Libvirt #Monitoring #CloudOperations #OzarLand
```

## PG-06 · "Compute down" does not mean the host is down

Image: [`dist/pg-06-compute-down-is-not-host-down.png`](dist/pg-06-compute-down-is-not-host-down.png)

```text
openstack compute service list shows a compute "down". What does Nova actually know?

Only this: it has heard nothing from the nova-compute agent of that host for service_down_time, 60 seconds by default. Nothing about the host. Nothing about the instances.

When only the agent stopped, the hypervisor and the instances run on, and users notice nothing. The danger is the operator, or the automation, that treats it as a dead host: evacuating now starts a second copy of every instance, writing to the same volumes.

Before anything else:
→ does the host answer ping and SSH?
→ does virsh list show the domains running?

If yes: fix the agent. Never evacuate.

Runbook: https://github.com/OzarLand/openstack-vm-runbooks/blob/main/recovery/nova-compute-down-instances-still-running.md
More memos: https://github.com/OzarLand/production-guide

#OpenStack #Nova #HighAvailability #CloudOperations #SRE #OzarLand
```

## PG-07 · Fence before you evacuate. Always.

Image: [`dist/pg-07-fence-before-evacuate.png`](dist/pg-07-fence-before-evacuate.png)

```text
A compute host stops answering. The instances on it are down. The pressure to run "server evacuate" is immediate.

But Nova cannot tell a dead host from an unreachable one. If the host is only cut off from the control plane, its instances may still be running, and still writing. Evacuate now and each volume gets two writers.

The order that makes it safe:
1. Confirm out of band (BMC, switch port, storage side)
2. Fence: power off, or isolate every port
3. Disable the service, force it down only now
4. Evacuate

The same goes for auto-evacuation tooling: if it reacts to a lost heartbeat without fencing, it will one day destroy the workload it was meant to save.

The precondition for evacuation is fencing, not a missing heartbeat.

Runbook: https://github.com/OzarLand/openstack-vm-runbooks/blob/main/recovery/compute-host-failure-fence-before-evacuate.md
More memos: https://github.com/OzarLand/production-guide

#OpenStack #Nova #HighAvailability #DisasterRecovery #CloudOperations #OzarLand
```

## PG-08 · Compute service: disabled and down are two different things

Image: [`dist/pg-08-disabled-or-down.png`](dist/pg-08-disabled-or-down.png)

```text
openstack compute service list shows two fields for every nova-compute. They are independent, and mixing them up is how instances get lost.

Status (enabled / disabled) answers: may the scheduler place new instances here?
It is a scheduling decision. Running instances are not affected.

State (up / down) answers: does Nova believe the service is alive?
It comes from the heartbeat, or from an operator who forced it down.

The danger is in what Nova allows once a service is down: deleting an instance becomes a local delete (the guest is not touched), and evacuation is allowed.

So never force down a compute that is not fenced. And before you re-enable one, read the disable reason: a reason starting with "AUTO:" was set by the libvirt driver and clears itself.

Runbook: https://github.com/OzarLand/openstack-vm-runbooks/blob/main/scheduling/compute-service-disabled-or-forced-down.md
More memos: https://github.com/OzarLand/production-guide

#OpenStack #Nova #CloudOperations #SRE #InfrastructureEngineering #OzarLand
```

## PG-09 · Emptying a compute host: one operation does not fit every instance

Image: [`dist/pg-09-emptying-a-host-for-maintenance.png`](dist/pg-09-emptying-a-host-for-maintenance.png)

```text
A compute needs a reboot for a kernel or QEMU patch. "Just live-migrate everything" is rarely the whole answer.

The operation depends on the instance:
→ shared storage or boot from volume: live migration
→ local disk: live block migration, the disk travels over the network
→ memory changing faster than it copies: auto-converge or post-copy, else cold migration
→ PCI passthrough, SR-IOV, vGPU: cold migration or restart, depending on your release

And one trap of every patching campaign: migration from a newer libvirt/QEMU to an older one is not supported. Once a host is patched, instances can move onto it, but not back. The order of patching decides where instances can go.

Nova cannot tell you which workload tolerates a pause or a restart. The owning teams can.

Runbook: https://github.com/OzarLand/openstack-vm-runbooks/blob/main/migration/moving-instances-off-a-host-for-maintenance.md
More memos: https://github.com/OzarLand/production-guide

#OpenStack #Nova #LiveMigration #Patching #CloudOperations #OzarLand
```

## PG-10 · ACTIVE, no fault, no IP address: Nova did its job

Image: [`dist/pg-10-active-but-no-ip.png`](dist/pg-10-active-but-no-ip.png)

```text
A new instance is ACTIVE. No fault. Nothing in the Nova logs. And nobody can reach it.

Instances created yesterday are fine, which makes it look like a problem with this one VM. It is not.

With ML2/OVS, a new port must be added to dnsmasq by a DHCP agent. If no agent is alive, the guest asks for a lease and never gets an answer. Running instances keep theirs (24 hours by default), so the outage is invisible until someone creates an instance.

Where to look:
→ the console log of the guest: DHCP asked, never answered
→ openstack network agent list --agent-type dhcp

ACTIVE means Nova did its job. It says nothing about the network of the guest.

Runbook: https://github.com/OzarLand/openstack-vm-runbooks/blob/main/networking/new-instance-gets-no-ip-dhcp-agents-down.md
More memos: https://github.com/OzarLand/production-guide

#OpenStack #Neutron #Networking #CloudOperations #SRE #OzarLand
```

## PG-11 · Reachable from inside, not from outside: walk the path in order

Image: [`dist/pg-11-unreachable-from-outside.png`](dist/pg-11-unreachable-from-outside.png)

```text
The instance got its address and its metadata. A neighbour in the same network reaches it. From outside: timeout.

This is rarely a mystery. It is four records to check, from the outside in:
1. Security group: is there an ingress rule for this protocol, port and source?
2. Floating IP: is it on this port, and on this fixed address?
3. Router: an interface on the subnet, and an external gateway?
4. The guest: its own firewall, a service actually listening?

Most cases end at 1 or 2.

One classic trap: an ingress rule whose remote is a security group, not a prefix. It admits members of that group only. That is exactly why the neighbour gets in and the outside does not.

Runbook: https://github.com/OzarLand/openstack-vm-runbooks/blob/main/networking/instance-unreachable-from-outside.md
More memos: https://github.com/OzarLand/production-guide

#OpenStack #Neutron #Networking #SecurityGroups #CloudOperations #OzarLand
```

## PG-12 · Ping works, large transfers stall: test the largest packet

Image: [`dist/pg-12-ping-works-transfers-stall.png`](dist/pg-12-ping-works-transfers-stall.png)

```text
Users say the service is "slow" or "hangs". Ping answers. SSH logs in, then freezes on a large output. Agents are alive, instances ACTIVE, the logs are clean.

On one compute, the interface that carries the VXLAN tunnels has a smaller MTU than Neutron assumes. Small packets still fit once encapsulated. Full-size packets do not, and are dropped without any error.

One test shows it, a don't-fragment ping at two sizes:
→ ping -M do -s 56: answered
→ ping -M do -s <network MTU - 28>: 100% loss

The rule: the tunnel interface MTU must be at least the network MTU plus 50 bytes for VXLAN over IPv4.

A green ping only proves that small packets pass.

Runbook: https://github.com/OzarLand/openstack-vm-runbooks/blob/main/networking/tunnel-mtu-mismatch-large-packets-dropped.md
More memos: https://github.com/OzarLand/production-guide

#OpenStack #Neutron #Networking #MTU #VXLAN #OzarLand
```

## PG-13 · Volume stuck in attaching or detaching: four views, one truth

Image: [`dist/pg-13-volume-stuck-attaching-or-detaching.png`](dist/pg-13-volume-stuck-attaching-or-detaching.png)

```text
A volume sits in "attaching" or "detaching" and every retry is refused. The tempting fix is one command: reset its state.

That command only rewrites Cinder's database record. It checks nothing. If a hypervisor still has the volume open, the next attach gives it a second writer, and two writers corrupt a filesystem.

Before any fix, compare four views of the same attachment:
→ Cinder: the volume status
→ Cinder: the attachment records
→ Nova: the server's volume list
→ the hypervisor: virsh domblklist

Three of them are database records. One is reality. The fix depends on which ones disagree.

The data is safe as long as nothing forces the state.

Runbook: https://github.com/OzarLand/openstack-vm-runbooks/blob/main/volumes/volume-stuck-in-attaching-or-detaching.md
More memos: https://github.com/OzarLand/production-guide

#OpenStack #Cinder #Nova #Storage #CloudOperations #OzarLand
```

## PG-14 · A volume still in-use for an instance that no longer exists

Image: [`dist/pg-14-volume-in-use-by-a-missing-instance.png`](dist/pg-14-volume-in-use-by-a-missing-instance.png)

```text
The instance was deleted, or evacuated. Its volume is still "in-use", attached to something that is gone. It cannot be deleted. It cannot be attached anywhere else.

The data is intact. The risk is entirely in the fix.

An attachment record is stale only if the hypervisor agrees:
→ instance gone from Nova, no domain on its last host uses the volume: stale, left by the deletion
→ the attachment ID is the one Nova's server volume list shows: in use, keep it
→ the instance runs on host B, the connector names host A: stale, left by the evacuation

Forcing the volume back to "available" checks none of this. If a hypervisor still has it open, the next attach creates a second writer.

Check the host before you touch the database.

Runbook: https://github.com/OzarLand/openstack-vm-runbooks/blob/main/volumes/stale-volume-attachment-after-instance-deleted-or-evacuated.md
More memos: https://github.com/OzarLand/production-guide

#OpenStack #Cinder #Storage #DataIntegrity #CloudOperations #OzarLand
```

## PG-15 · Control plane down is not the same as workloads down

Image: [`dist/pg-15-control-plane-down.png`](dist/pg-15-control-plane-down.png)

```text
The APIs do not answer. The message bus is broken. The database is unavailable. Is production down?

Not necessarily. The control plane and the data plane fail separately, and the data plane does not need the APIs to carry the state it already has.

What keeps working:
→ running instances, their disks, their traffic
→ existing DHCP leases
→ security groups, floating IPs and routes already programmed

What is lost:
→ create, change, migrate, delete
→ any new state reaching the data plane
→ metadata for instances that boot or reboot
→ consoles, and monitoring that reads the APIs

This is what makes "protect the running workloads, then repair" a real option. But it depends on your networking backend: verify it on a lab before the incident, and write the result down.

Runbook: https://github.com/OzarLand/openstack-vm-runbooks/blob/main/diagnostics/control-plane-down-what-still-works-for-instances.md
More memos: https://github.com/OzarLand/production-guide

#OpenStack #ControlPlane #IncidentResponse #CloudOperations #SRE #OzarLand
```

## PG-16 · MessagingTimeout in every service: diagnose the bus before the services

Image: [`dist/pg-16-rpc-timeouts-everywhere.png`](dist/pg-16-rpc-timeouts-everywhere.png)

```text
MessagingTimeout in Nova. In Neutron. In Cinder. Computes reported down although nova-compute is running. Agents flapping.

When every service shows the same symptom at once, the services are rarely the cause. Look at what they share: the message bus.

On every RabbitMQ node, read-only:
→ one node missing, the others agree: a node is down
→ nodes disagree, or partitions listed: a network partition
→ a memory or disk alarm: publishers are blocked, cluster-wide
→ RPC queues growing with 0 consumers: the bus is fine, a service is gone

Four cases, four different responses. And one thing to keep for last: resetting RabbitMQ deletes every queue and every message.

Running instances keep running through all of this.

Runbook: https://github.com/OzarLand/openstack-vm-runbooks/blob/main/recovery/rabbitmq-partition-or-alarm-rpc-timeouts.md
More memos: https://github.com/OzarLand/production-guide

#OpenStack #RabbitMQ #ControlPlane #IncidentResponse #CloudOperations #OzarLand
```

## PG-17 · Galera lost quorum: the data is at risk during the recovery, not before

Image: [`dist/pg-17-galera-lost-quorum.png`](dist/pg-17-galera-lost-quorum.png)

```text
Every OpenStack API fails or hangs. The logs say "WSREP has not yet prepared node for application use".

Galera accepts writes only in a Primary component, a majority of the last known nodes. Lose the majority and the remaining nodes refuse queries. That is a safety mechanism, not the failure.

Running instances keep running. And the data is not at risk yet. It becomes at risk during the recovery, if the cluster is bootstrapped from a node that is not the most advanced: the transactions only the other nodes had are discarded, for good.

So before any recovery command, on every node:
→ is MariaDB running?
→ wsrep_cluster_status: Primary or non-Primary?
→ wsrep_last_committed: how far did this node get?

One node down, quorum lost and full stop are three different cases with three different answers.

Runbook: https://github.com/OzarLand/openstack-vm-runbooks/blob/main/recovery/galera-cluster-lost-quorum-database-unavailable.md
More memos: https://github.com/OzarLand/production-guide

#OpenStack #MariaDB #Galera #ControlPlane #DatabaseReliability #OzarLand
```

## PG-18 · Restarting libvirt or the OVS agent: will the instances survive?

Image: [`dist/pg-18-before-restarting-an-agent.png`](dist/pg-18-before-restarting-an-agent.png)

```text
"I need to restart libvirt on a compute that runs 40 instances. Will they stop?"

The answer comes from knowing which process actually carries the workload.

libvirtd: the qemu processes are processes of the host, not children locked inside the container. A new libvirtd re-attaches to them. It holds only if the container runs in the host's PID namespace.

Open vSwitch agent: it does not carry traffic, ovs-vswitchd does. The agent only programs flows, and they stay in place while it restarts. It holds only if drop_flows_on_start is False, the default.

In both cases something does wait during the restart: builds, migrations, new ports, security group changes.

One setting each stands between "nobody noticed" and "every instance on the host stopped". Check it before, not after.

Runbook: https://github.com/OzarLand/openstack-vm-runbooks/blob/main/lifecycle/restarting-nova-libvirt-does-not-stop-instances.md
More memos: https://github.com/OzarLand/production-guide
```

## PG-19 · A VM creation failed. Follow one request id, not the timestamps.

Image: [`dist/pg-19-trace-one-request.png`](dist/pg-19-trace-one-request.png)

```text
A failed VM creation tells you what the user experienced. It does not tell you which service caused it.

A scheduling problem looks like a Nova problem. A network timeout looks like a Neutron problem. The architecture makes each one plausible without making any of them true.

One build traverses Keystone, nova-api, the conductor and scheduler with Placement, nova-compute on the selected host, then Glance, Neutron and libvirt. Every API request carries a request id that the services propagate in their logs.

So:
1. get the request id from the server's events
2. grep it through the services, in path order
3. the last service that logged it is where the request stopped

Then compare with a request that succeeded. Same host? Same network? Same image? The difference is the lead.

Runbook: https://github.com/OzarLand/openstack-vm-runbooks/blob/main/diagnostics/what-a-vm-creation-traverses-and-tracing-by-request-id.md
```

## PG-20 · Stale records: project tools first, the database last

Image: [`dist/pg-20-cleaning-up-stale-records.png`](dist/pg-20-cleaning-up-stale-records.png)

```text
A long-lived platform accumulates records that describe nothing real. Instances in BUILD for days. Ports whose instance is gone. Volumes attached to nothing. Placement allocations for consumers that no longer exist.

No direct outage, which is why it is neglected. But they hold quota, distort capacity, and make every investigation start with the same question: is this record true?

The clean-up is a ladder. Climb only as high as you must:
1. Read-only audit
2. The API: reset the state, then delete through the API
3. The *-manage tools, with --dry-run first
4. The database: last resort, with a backup, one row at a time

A direct database edit bypasses every consistency check the services perform. It is rarely the shortest path it appears to be.

Runbook: https://github.com/OzarLand/openstack-vm-runbooks/blob/main/lifecycle/stale-records-stuck-instances-orphan-ports-attachments.md
More memos: https://github.com/OzarLand/production-guide
```

## PG-21 · An instance went SHUTOFF by itself. Nova did not stop it: the kernel did.

Image: [`dist/pg-21-shutoff-by-itself.png`](dist/pg-21-shutoff-by-itself.png)

```text
An instance that was ACTIVE is SHUTOFF. Its owner did not stop it. And yet its action list shows a "stop".

That stop was made by Nova itself, after the fact. The real sequence:
→ the compute ran out of memory
→ the kernel's OOM killer killed a QEMU process
→ libvirt reported the guest as stopped
→ nova-compute aligned its record by calling the stop API

Nova does not restart the guest. It stays SHUTOFF until someone starts it, and it boots like after a power loss.

The usual root cause is not the instance. It is the inventory: reserved_host_memory_mb left at its 512 MB default on a host whose own services use several GB. The scheduler fills the compute up to a number the host cannot honour.

Source runbook status: draft. Read its limits before acting.

Runbook: https://github.com/OzarLand/openstack-vm-runbooks/blob/main/lifecycle/instance-shut-off-by-host-oom-killer.md
More memos: https://github.com/OzarLand/production-guide
```

## PG-22 · VERIFY_RESIZE is not a stuck state. It is a pending decision.

Image: [`dist/pg-22-resize-not-finished.png`](dist/pg-22-resize-not-finished.png)

```text
After a resize or a cold migration, an instance can sit in three states that look alike on a dashboard and mean very different things.

→ VERIFY_RESIZE, no task state: the resize worked. It waits for a confirm or a revert, and can wait for days.
→ RESIZE, with a task state: the operation stopped part way. A service died, or a message was lost.
→ ERROR: a step failed, and the fault says which one.

The first is the one that surprises people. While an instance stays in VERIFY_RESIZE, the old copy is kept on the source and Placement holds resources on both computes. Many of them make hosts look fuller than they are.

And neither way out can be undone: confirm deletes the old copy, revert loses what the guest wrote to its local disks since the resize. That decision belongs to the owner.

Runbook: https://github.com/OzarLand/openstack-vm-runbooks/blob/main/lifecycle/resize-stuck-in-verify-resize-or-failed.md
More memos: https://github.com/OzarLand/production-guide

#OpenStack #Nova #Placement #CloudOperations #SRE #OzarLand
```

## PG-23 · A live migration that never completes: watch one number

Image: [`dist/pg-23-live-migration-never-completes.png`](dist/pg-23-live-migration-never-completes.png)

```text
A live migration starts fine. Then it runs. And runs. Much longer than the others. Eventually the instance is ACTIVE again, on the source, and the migration is marked failed.

Live migration copies memory while the instance keeps running. Every page written again must be copied again. If the instance dirties memory faster than the network copies it, the migration cannot converge.

One number tells you which case you are in, memory_remaining_bytes:
→ it falls steadily, slowly: a slow or shared migration network
→ it falls, then hovers: it will not converge without help

The ways out all have a price. Force-complete pauses the instance. Auto-converge throttles its CPU. Post-copy completes, but a network break during that phase reboots the instance.

Source runbook status: draft, not yet reproduced on a lab.

Runbook: https://github.com/OzarLand/openstack-vm-runbooks/blob/main/migration/live-migration-never-completes-or-times-out.md
```

## PG-24 · Every instance on one compute lost its network. Nova says ACTIVE.

Image: [`dist/pg-24-whole-compute-lost-network.png`](dist/pg-24-whole-compute-lost-network.png)

```text
Every instance on one compute stops answering. Ping, SSH, application traffic: nothing.

Nova shows all of them ACTIVE, power state Running. And Nova is right, from where it stands: it reads the state of instances from libvirt, and libvirt still runs them.

The process that actually switches their traffic, ovs-vswitchd, has stopped.

Three views of the same compute:
→ Nova: ACTIVE, Running
→ Neutron: the Open vSwitch agent is not alive (a consequence, and it can take a minute to show)
→ the compute: ovs-vswitchd does not answer

The trap is to restart the agent, because it is the one reported dead. The agent only programs flows. Start ovs-vswitchd, and the agent recovers by itself.

Monitoring built on Nova states cannot see a data-plane outage.

Runbook: https://github.com/OzarLand/openstack-vm-runbooks/blob/main/networking/ovs-vswitchd-down-on-compute.md
More memos: https://github.com/OzarLand/production-guide

#OpenStack #Neutron #OpenvSwitch #Monitoring #CloudOperations #OzarLand
```

## PG-25 · A security group rule that changes nothing: four things to check

Image: [`dist/pg-25-security-group-rule-has-no-effect.png`](dist/pg-25-security-group-rule-has-no-effect.png)

```text
You add a rule. The port stays closed. Or you remove one, and the traffic still gets through.

Before blaming the agent, remember how security groups work: allow rules only, on a default deny, and the groups on a port add up. Then check four things.

→ The rule is on a group the port does not use, or it does not match: direction, ethertype (an IPv4 rule for IPv6 traffic), port range, or a remote group the traffic does not come from.
→ Port security is off on the port: no rule applies at all, everything passes.
→ The agent on the compute is dead: the rule exists in the API, the compute still holds the old ones.
→ Both instances are in "default": that group admits its own members, by design.

Three of these four are not a platform fault.
```

## PG-26 · 503 from the API: HAProxy is the messenger, not the cause

Image: [`dist/pg-26-api-returns-503.png`](dist/pg-26-api-returns-503.png)

```text
"503 Service Unavailable: No server is available to handle this request."

That sentence does not come from Nova or Keystone. It comes from HAProxy, and it means one precise thing: no backend of that API is passing its health check.

What HAProxy shows tells you where to go next:
→ every server DOWN with L4CON: the service is down on every controller. Its own log says why.
→ servers DOWN with L7TOUT or L7STS: the service runs but cannot answer. It is stuck on a dependency.
→ one server DOWN, the others UP: one controller. Users see nothing.
→ the VIP on no node, or on two: keepalived, not a backend.

The tempting fix is to restart things at the front door. But restarting a service whose database is unreachable only loses the requests in flight.

Running instances keep running through all of it.

Runbook: https://github.com/OzarLand/openstack-vm-runbooks/blob/main/recovery/api-returns-503-haproxy-backend-down-or-vip-flapping.md
More memos: https://github.com/OzarLand/production-guide
```

## PG-27 · 401 with a token that should be valid: the fresh token is lying to you

Image: [`dist/pg-27-401-with-a-valid-token.png`](dist/pg-27-401-with-a-valid-token.png)

```text
openstack token issue works. The next command fails with 401. Then works. Then fails.

Behind a load balancer, that pattern means one Keystone node cannot validate tokens the others issued. Two usual reasons, and they do not hit the same tokens:

→ Fernet keys differ between nodes: it breaks tokens older than the token cache, 10 minutes by default. Long-running clients, scripts, Horizon sessions.
→ A clock is off on one node: it breaks fresh tokens too.

Here is the trap. Keystone caches every token it issues in a cache shared by all nodes. For 10 minutes, any node answers from the cache, without decrypting anything. So your test with a brand new token passes on every node, with diverged keys.

Test with a token older than the cache. And compare key checksums across nodes, not key numbers.

Runbook: https://github.com/OzarLand/openstack-vm-runbooks/blob/main/recovery/keystone-401-for-every-request-fernet-keys-or-clock.md
More memos: https://github.com/OzarLand/production-guide

#OpenStack #Keystone #Authentication #ControlPlane #CloudOperations #OzarLand
```

## PG-28 · "Too many connections": three limits, three messages

Image: [`dist/pg-28-database-connections-exhausted.png`](dist/pg-28-database-connections-exhausted.png)

```text
API calls fail with 500. The logs talk about database connections. The reflex is to raise a limit somewhere.

With MariaDB behind ProxySQL, there are three places where connections can run out, and each has its own message:

→ "QueuePool limit of size ... reached": the SQLAlchemy pool inside one service. The database is fine. That service holds its sessions too long.
→ "9001 Max connect timeout reached": ProxySQL could not get a backend connection in time.
→ "1040 Too many connections": MariaDB itself, or ProxySQL's client side.

Read the message before touching a setting. A larger pool per process, multiplied by the number of processes and controllers, simply moves the limit one layer down.

And one false friend: 9001 with no writer online is a Galera problem, not a connection problem.

Source runbook status: draft.

Runbook: https://github.com/OzarLand/openstack-vm-runbooks/blob/main/recovery/database-too-many-connections-or-pool-exhausted.md
More memos: https://github.com/OzarLand/production-guide

#OpenStack #MariaDB #ProxySQL #ControlPlane #CloudOperations #OzarLand
```
